resources.string: Check engine
Warning light and stored codes
Tells whether the check engine light is on and how many stored codes the computer has.
No faults: light off and zero codes.
With the light on, open Fault codes to see which ones. If it flashes it is a serious misfire: slow down and get it checked soon.
Fuel system
Normal = already adjusting with the O2 sensor
How the computer is mixing fuel: adjusting with the oxygen sensor (closed loop) or without it (open loop).
Cold, a few minutes in open loop; once warm, Normal (closed loop).
If it does not reach Normal with a warm engine, an oxygen sensor or the temperature sensor may be failing.
Engine load
How hard the engine is working
Percentage of the most air the engine could take in at those RPM. A measure of how much effort it is making.
Idle 20–35 %. Flat-road cruise 25–50 %. Hard acceleration near 100 %.
High at idle (over 40 %) can be the A/C or a large electrical load; otherwise a vacuum leak.
Coolant temp.
Normal 85–105 °C when warm
Temperature of the engine coolant. The most important reading to protect the engine.
85–105 °C when warm. Takes 5–10 min to get there. The fan usually starts near 100 °C.
Over 110 °C: pull over and stop the engine; coolant may be low or the fan or thermostat may have failed. If it never exceeds 70–75 °C, the thermostat is stuck open (uses more fuel).
Short-term fuel trim
Instant correction; normal ±10 %
How much fuel the computer is adding or removing right now to keep the mixture ideal.
Swings around 0 %, within ±10 %.
Stuck above +10 %: lean mixture (extra air or too little fuel). Stuck below –10 %: rich mixture (leaking injector or clogged air filter).
Long-term fuel trim
Learned correction; beyond ±10 % is a fault
The correction the computer learned over time to compensate for wear or leaks.
Near 0 %, within ±10 %.
Above +10 %: extra air or too little fuel (vacuum leak, pump, filter). Below –10 %: too much fuel.
Fuel pressure
Fuel rail pressure
Pressure with which the pump sends fuel to the injectors.
Between 250 and 450 kPa on most port-injection cars; much higher on direct injection.
Low: weak pump or clogged filter (the car stumbles). High: faulty regulator.
Intake pressure (MAP)
Manifold vacuum; low at idle
Air pressure inside the intake manifold. The computer uses it to work out how much air is coming in.
Idle 25–45 kPa. Rises when accelerating; at full load near air pressure (100 kPa), more with a turbo.
High at idle: vacuum leak or faulty sensor. If it never changes, the sensor is stuck.
RPM
Engine revolutions
How many turns per minute the crankshaft makes.
Idle 600–900 rpm when warm. Highway 1,800–3,000 rpm.
Idle that hunts or is very low: sensor, dirty throttle body or vacuum leak.
Speed
What the engine computer measures
Vehicle speed according to the computer, from the wheel or transmission sensor.
Same as the dashboard speedometer (the dash usually reads a little higher).
If it reads 0 while moving, the speed sensor failed.
Ignition timing
Degrees before top dead center
How long before the piston reaches the top the spark fires.
At idle 5–20°; rises with RPM and falls with load.
Very retarded or fixed: the computer is protecting the engine (knock, bad fuel or a sensor).
Intake air temp.
Air entering the engine; near ambient
Temperature of the air entering the engine.
Close to the outside temperature; a bit higher with a hot engine at a stop.
Much higher than ambient while moving: hot air intake or faulty sensor.
Air flow (MAF)
Used to work out consumption
Grams of air entering the engine per second.
Idle 2–6 g/s on a 1.6–2.0 L engine; rises with RPM.
Too low for the RPM: dirty sensor. MAF cleaner usually fixes it.
Throttle
Throttle opening
How open the throttle plate is.
Idle 10–20 %. Floored, near 100 %.
If it rises by itself at idle, the throttle body is dirty or the sensor is failing.
Oxygen sensors
How many the exhaust has
How many oxygen sensors the car\'s exhaust has.
Two (before and after the catalytic converter) on a four-cylinder; four on a V6 or V8.
It does not change while you drive.
Oxygen sensor 1
Before the catalytic converter; swings 0.1–0.9 V
Measures whether the mixture is rich or lean before the catalytic converter.
Swings quickly between 0.1 and 0.9 V with a warm engine.
Stuck at one value or very slow: old sensor or mixture out of control.
Oxygen sensor 2
After the catalytic converter; steady
Measures the exhaust after the catalytic converter to tell whether it works.
Steady around 0.4–0.8 V.
If it swings like the first one, the converter no longer cleans (code P0420).
OBD standard
Standard the car complies with
The on-board diagnostics standard the car complies with.
OBD-II on cars in Mexico and the US; EOBD in Europe.
It does not change.
Time since start
Since the engine was started
Seconds the engine has run since the last start.
Starts at 0 when you start and counts up.
If it resets by itself while driving, the engine stalled and restarted.
Distance with check engine
Driven with the light on
Kilometers driven with the warning light on.
0 km if it has never been on.
If it grows, you have been driving with a fault: get it checked.
Evaporative purge
Tank vapors being burned
How far the valve that sends fuel vapor from the tank to the engine is open.
Closed when cold and at idle; opens while driving warm.
Always closed or always open: stuck purge valve (can set P044x codes).
Fuel level
Fuel in the tank
How much fuel is in the tank according to the float.
Drops slowly; rises when you fill up.
Jumps around: the float is failing. Some cars do not report this.
Warm-ups since clear
Cold starts counted
Times the engine fully warmed up since the codes were cleared.
Goes up by one per long trip.
If it is 0 or very low, codes were cleared or the battery was disconnected recently.
Distance since clear
Driven since the codes were cleared
Kilometers driven since the codes were cleared or the battery was disconnected.
Grows as you drive.
If it is very low, the emissions monitors may not have finished yet.
Barometric pressure
Drops with altitude (1,600 m ≈ 85 kPa)
Outside air pressure as measured by the car.
101 kPa at sea level; about 85 kPa at 1,600 m; about 77 kPa at 2,240 m.
If it does not drop going up a mountain, the sensor failed.
Catalyst temp.
Before the converter (bank 1)
Temperature of the exhaust gases entering the catalytic converter.
Between 300 and 800 °C while driving.
Over 900 °C: rich mixture or misfire; it can damage the converter.
Control module voltage
With the engine running ~13.5–14.5 V
Battery voltage as seen by the computer.
Off ~12.4–12.8 V. Engine running 13.5–14.5 V.
Below 13 V while running: the alternator is not charging. Above 15 V: faulty regulator.
Absolute load
Air per cylinder versus the maximum
Air entering per engine cycle as a percentage of the theoretical maximum.
Idle 15–30 %; hard acceleration 80–100 %, more with a turbo.
High at idle: vacuum leak or sensor fault.
Commanded mixture (λ)
1.00 = ideal; <1 rich, >1 lean
Air-fuel mixture the computer is asking for, in lambda.
1.00 at cruise. Below 1 under hard acceleration; above 1 when decelerating.
Stuck far from 1.00 with a warm engine: faulty oxygen or air sensor.
Relative throttle
Opening versus the learned minimum
Throttle opening counted from the closed position the computer learned.
0 % at idle; 100 % floored.
Not 0 % at idle: dirty throttle body or it needs to relearn.
Ambient temp.
Outside air
Outside air temperature according to the car\'s sensor.
Close to the actual weather.
Very different from the real weather: sensor heated by the engine (normal after stopping) or faulty.
Throttle (sensor B)
Second throttle sensor
Second throttle position sensor; the computer compares it with the first.
Similar to throttle A (may be mirrored).
If it does not match A, one of the two sensors is failing.
Pedal (sensor D)
How far you press the accelerator
Position of the electronic accelerator pedal.
0–20 % untouched; rises as you press.
If it does not return to 0 % when released, the pedal or its sensor is failing.
Pedal (sensor E)
Redundant pedal sensor
Second pedal sensor, used to check the first.
Similar to sensor D.
If it does not match D, one of the two is failing.
Commanded throttle
What the computer asks it to open
Throttle opening the computer is requesting.
Should closely follow the actual throttle.
If the actual one does not catch up, the throttle body is dirty or faulty.
Time with check engine
Minutes with the light on
Minutes the engine has run with the warning light on.
0 min if it has never been on.
If it grows, there is an active fault that has not been dealt with.
Time since clear
Minutes since the codes were cleared
Engine minutes since the codes were cleared.
Grows as you drive.
Very low: codes were cleared or the battery was disconnected recently.
Oil temp.
Engine oil
Temperature of the engine oil.
80–110 °C when warm; takes longer than the coolant.
Over 130 °C: slow down; check oil level and quality.
Fuel rate
Liters per hour the engine uses
Fuel the engine is using at this moment.
Idle 0.6–1.2 L/h; highway 5–8 L/h.
Very high at idle: rich mixture or leaking injector.
No faults
Normal
Open loop
Faulted
Data %1$s
No description
The car reports this value, but LiteDash cannot explain it yet.
No reference.
No reference.
